# Task 2 — Velocity-Characterization Pipeline Verification (Vx)

**Date:** 2026-08-06
**Scope:** Two-part verification of the robot velocity-characterization analysis
pipeline in `analysis/` (pid_tuner.py, csv_analyzer.py).
**Tools used (NOT modified):** `analysis/pid_tuner.py`, `analysis/csv_analyzer.py`
(only numpy/matplotlib, both pre-installed).

---

## Part A — Synthetic fixture: prove the tools recover a known plant

### A.1 Fixtures (generated by `analysis/tests/make_fixture_engine_vx.py`, seeded RNG)

All three fixtures use the exact Engine-logger header
`ElapsedTime,RobotID,Team,Vx_Command,Vy_Command,Angular_Command,Pos_X,Pos_Y,Orientation,Vx_Actual,Vy_Actual`
and plant `Vx_Actual = 0 for t < t_step+L`, then
`K·A·(1 − exp(−(t−t_step−L)/T))`, `K=0.95, A=1.0`, zero-mean noise σ=0.01,
`Pos_X = cumsum(Vx_Actual·dt)`, `Vy_Command=Angular_Command=Orientation=Vy_Actual=0`.

| Fixture | dt | L_true | T_true | rows | step1 (0→1.0) | step2 scaffold (1.0→0.5) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fixture_engine_vx_step.csv` | 60 Hz (16.667 ms) | 0.030 s | 0.120 s | 85 | t=0.350 s | t=1.150 s |
| `fixture_engine_vx_step_verif.csv` | 60 Hz | 0.300 s | 0.200 s | 130 | t=0.350 s | t=2.100 s |
| `fixture_engine_vx_step_1khz.csv` | 1 kHz (1 ms) | 0.030 s | 0.120 s | 1166 | t=0.350 s | t=1.150 s |

**Two documented deviations from the ideal spec (required by tool constraints, not by physics):**
1. First step at **t=0.350 s** instead of 0.300 s — both tools' step detector
   (`MIN_SAMPLES=20`, pid_tuner.py:105 / csv_analyzer.py:52) needs ≥20 samples on
   the pre-step plateau; at 60 Hz that is ≥0.333 s, so 0.300 s is undetectable.
2. A **second, short step** (1.0→0.5) closes the step *pair* both tools require
   (`len(steps) < 2 → "No step transitions found"`). Its tail is kept under
   20 samples so exactly the first (0→1.0) step is analyzed and only that step
   is the recovery evidence.

### A.2 Recovery results — `pid_tuner.py <fixture> -c Vx_Command -m Vx_Actual --open-loop -n`

| Fixture | Param | True | Recovered | Error | Within ±15%? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| spec @60 Hz | K | 0.950 | 0.9447 | **−0.6%** | ✅ |
| | L | 0.030 s | 0.0667 s | **+122%** | ❌ |
| | T | 0.120 s | 0.1000 s | **−16.7%** | ❌ |
| verif @60 Hz | K | 0.950 | 0.9391 | **−1.1%** | ✅ |
| | L | 0.300 s | 0.3333 s | **+11.1%** | ✅ |
| | T | 0.200 s | 0.1833 s | **−8.4%** | ✅ |
| spec @1 kHz | K | 0.950 | 0.9456 | **−0.5%** | ✅ |
| | L | 0.030 s | 0.0370 s | **+23.3%** | ❌ |
| | T | 0.120 s | 0.1140 s | **−5.0%** | ✅ |

**Conclusion:** the tools **do recover a known FOPDT plant** (verif row: all three
parameters within ±15% on the engine logger's real 60 Hz rate). `K` recovers
robustly in every case (<1% error, noise-limited). The spec'd fast plant
(L=30 ms, T=120 ms) cannot meet the ±15% dead-time target at 60 Hz — **the
sample rate is too low for the dead time** (30 ms ≈ 1.8 samples; the recovered
L is quantized to the 16.7 ms grid) **and the tool's L definition itself
includes the 5 % rise time of the first-order response** (`L_est ≈ L_true +
0.0513·T + 1 sample`). The 1 kHz row proves this second part: even at 1 kHz the
30 ms dead time is over-estimated by +23 % because `0.0513·T = 6.2 ms` is
inherent to the 5 %-crossing method, so `L` needs `L ≳ 0.0513·T` to be
recoverable to ±15 % (at 60 Hz the grid adds another ≤33 ms).

### A.3 Step metrics — `csv_analyzer.py <fixture> -c Vx_Command --export <json>`

Vx_Actual metrics (all non-NaN and sensible):

| Fixture | gain | rise_time_ms | overshoot_pct | settle_2pct_ms | latency_ms | clipped | noisy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| spec @60 Hz | 0.9447 | 166.7 | 1.28 | 550.0 | 0.0* | false | false |
| verif @60 Hz | 0.9391 | 516.7 | 1.97 | 1083.3 | 333.3 | false | false |
| spec @1 kHz | 0.9456 | 151.0 | 3.14 | 793.0 | 28.0 | false | false |

*`latency_ms=0.0` is a tool quirk: `latency_analysis` (csv_analyzer.py:352) takes
the mean of the *first 10 samples after step_start* as baseline, which overlaps
the rising response (response starts ≈3 samples after the window start), so the
first sample already exceeds the 5 % threshold → 0 ms. Not a data problem.

## Part B — Real-data dry run (`TestescalonVx.csv`, 7117 rows @ 1 kHz, jul 8)

Command `v_vel[0]` (auto/forced `-c v_vel[0]`), measurement `vx_est`.
Recording: `v_vel[0]` 0 → **47.386 s** 1.0 → **47.921 s** 0. Single step pair,
plateau = 0.535 s.

### B.1 Identified plant (FOPDT) — `pid_tuner.py TestescalonVx.csv -c v_vel[0] -m vx_est --open-loop`

```
Process gain K:  0.3805
Dead time  L:    95.0 ms
Time const T:    245.0 ms
T / L ratio:     2.6
```

csv_analyzer (vx_est) corroborates: gain 0.381, ss 0.381, rise 340 ms, overshoot
28.9 %, peak 0.49 @455 ms, settle 2 %/5 % 534 ms, `noisy=true`, `clipped=false`.

### ⚠️ CRITICAL CAVEAT — the plant input is a RAMP, not a step

The firmware ramps vx/vy commands at `ROBOT_MAX_LINEAR_ACC = 1.5 m/s²`
(7.5 mm/s per 5 ms cycle), so a 1.0 m/s step takes ~0.67 s to reach full value —
the effective plant input is a **ramp**, not a pure step. Fitted against a ramp,
FOPDT dead-time **L** and time-constant **T** are biased (they are **upper
bounds** on the true values), while the steady-state gain **K**
(Δresponse/Δinput) is the reliable parameter. **However**, in the jul-8
recording the command plateau (0.535 s) was *shorter* than the ramp duration
(0.667 s), so the input never reached 1.0 m/s (peak ≈ 1.5·0.535 = 0.80 m/s) and
the response never settled — the recovered **K = 0.381 is therefore a lower
bound**, and L=95 ms / T=245 ms are upper bounds. A new recording with a
plateau ≳ 2 s (and ≳ 5·T) is required for a reliable steady-state gain.

### B.2 Tuning rules (as printed by the tool)

| Method | Type | Kp | Ki | Kd |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ziegler-Nichols | P | 6.777 | 0 | 0 |
| Ziegler-Nichols | PI | 6.100 | 19.281 | 0 |
| Ziegler-Nichols | PID | 8.133 | 42.804 | 0.386 |
| Tyreus-Luyben | PI | 2.101 | 6.641 | 0 |
| Tyreus-Luyben | PID | 3.050 | 13.958 | 0.122 |
| IMC (default λ = max(0.25T, 2L) = 190 ms) | P | 2.259 | 0 | 0 |
| IMC (default λ) | PI | 2.259 | 9.221 | 0 |
| IMC (default λ) | PID | 2.259 | 9.221 | 0.107 |

### B.3 Recommended pid_vx gains — IMC-PI with conservative λ

**Choice: IMC-PI (no derivative), λ = T = 245 ms** → **Kp = 1.89, Ki = 7.73**.

Justification:
- **IMC over ZN:** ZN-PI (Kp=6.1, Ki=19.3) would demand 6.1 m/s of output for a
  1 m/s error (4× the 1.5 outputMax) and Ki·Ts = 0.096 per cycle — far too
  aggressive for a 200 Hz discrete loop on a noisy estimate. ZN is only a
  starting point, never a final choice here.
- **IMC over Tyreus-Luyben:** TL-PI (2.10, 6.64) is close, but TL is tuned for
  tight disturbance rejection on near-integrating processes; IMC gives an
  explicit robustness knob (λ) and its PI form is the natural controller for a
  stable FOPDT plant.
- **Conservative λ:** the plant fit is doubly pessimistic (L,T upper bounds;
  K lower bound), so a larger-than-minimum λ is warranted. `λ = T = 245 ms`
  (vs. the tool default `2L = 190 ms`) keeps the closed loop slower than the
  plant's uncertainty and still ≥2.9 rad/s bandwidth. With `λ = T`:
  `Kp = T/(K·(L+λ)) = 1.894`, `Ki = 1/(K·(L+λ)) = 7.730`.
- **200 Hz discrete check:** closed-loop bandwidth ≈ 1/(L+λ) = 2.94 rad/s →
  Ts·ω ≈ 0.015 ≪ 0.5; Ki·Ts = 0.039 per cycle. No discretization risk.
- **outputMax 1.5:** a 1 m/s error demands 1.89 m/s output → brief initial
  saturation (~79 % utilization) that matches the existing firmware behavior and
  is acceptable for a rate-limited command ramp.

### Comparison table vs. current firmware (Kp=2.5, Ki=9.2 in drive_task.c)

| Gains | Kp | Ki | Kd | Source / note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Current firmware | 2.5 | 9.2 | 0 | drive_task.c (verified) |
| Tool default IMC-PI (λ=2L=190 ms) | 2.259 | 9.221 | 0 | pid_tuner.py recommended line |
| **Recommended conservative IMC-PI (λ=T=245 ms)** | **1.89** | **7.73** | **0** | this analysis |
| IMC-PI λ=1.5T (very conservative) | 1.392 | 5.682 | 0 | lower bound of the sensible range |

Notably, the firmware's (2.5, 9.2) already sits essentially on the tool's
default IMC-PI (2.26, 9.22) — a good sign the in-field tuning converged to the
model-based answer. The conservative recommendation is a modest de-rating
(≈ −25 % Kp, −16 % Ki) consistent with the ramp-truncated plant estimate; the
firmware values remain defensible as-is.

## Tool limitations discovered (for future calibration runs)

1. **Dead-time resolution:** `L` is quantized to the sample grid and includes
   `0.0513·T` (5 %-crossing definition); at 60 Hz a <50 ms dead time is not
   recoverable, and even at 1 kHz L≪0.0513·T is over-estimated (Part A).
2. **Step-pair requirement:** both tools silently skip data with <2 detected
   steps (`MIN_SAMPLES=20` per segment); the real Vx log has exactly one
   command cycle, so only that single step was characterized.
3. **`K` assumes meas-baseline == cmd_before:** a second step (or any step after
   a settled state with steady-state error) gets a biased gain; the first
   0→A step is the only clean window. (Documented; avoided by fixture design.)
4. **`latency_ms` baseline quirk:** baseline = mean of first 10 samples after
   step_start; if the response starts within that window, latency reads 0 ms.
5. **Tool-interface note:** the task's csv_analyzer invocation included `-m vx_est`,
   but csv_analyzer.py has no `--meas` flag (it analyzes all measurement columns);
   it was run as `-c v_vel[0] --all-steps` and `vx_est` metrics are present in the
   JSON export. No tool was modified.
6. **Ramp-vs-step (this recording):** K is a lower bound because the 0.535 s
   plateau was shorter than the 0.667 s ramp — steady state was never reached.
